sources.news_title: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins wins Alaska governor's race
Democrat wins Alaska governor seat for first time in almost 30 years
sources.text:
Democrats have captured Alaska’s governor’s seat for the first time in nearly three decades, marking another major victory for their party in a midterm election period that has dramatically shifted political power across the US.
Former Alaska state legislator Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republican opponents, including a candidate backed by US president Donald Trump, becoming the first Democrat elected governor of Alaska since 1998.
His victory – called by the Associated Press on Friday, 10 days after the polls closed – adds to a growing list of Democratic gains nationwide, bringing the party’s total to 30 US governorships. Democrats have also taken control of governor’s offices in several other long-time Republican strongholds, including Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas.
Kreiss-Tomkins, widely known as JKT, secured the win having mounted a political comeback three years after departing the Alaska house of representatives.
READ MORE
The 37-year-old travelled extensively throughout the state during his campaign, building support around economic concerns and a promise to change the direction of Alaska’s government.
His platform centred on tackling affordability, ensuring full funding for public education, and requiring all oil and gas producers to pay corporate income taxes. He also pushed for a temporary halt to new data centre developments until state lawmakers establish regulations governing their construction.
Throughout the campaign, Kreiss-Tomkins sharply criticised the leadership of outgoing the Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, arguing that Alaska had become “broken” during his eight years in office.
“Alaskans are hungry for change,” Kreiss-Tomkins said. “We’ve been running the same campaign since we launched in February, and I don’t take anyone’s vote for granted.”
Among his criticisms was the deterioration of the state’s ferry system, which Kreiss-Tomkins said had been left in disarray as service to numerous communities was drastically reduced. The ferry network serves as a critical transportation link for communities in southeast Alaska that lack road connections, including some with limited access to air travel.
Despite his criticism of the outgoing administration, Kreiss-Tomkins presented himself as a leader willing to work across political divisions. He pledged to assemble a cabinet that includes Democrats, Republicans and independents.
Unlike most states, Alaska allows voters to rank candidates by preference through ranked-choice voting – a system that also permits multiple candidates from the same political party to run against one another.
But Kreiss-Tomkins avoided the need for additional rounds of vote counting after winning more than 50 per cent of first-choice votes, securing an outright victory.
The Alaska result comes just days after Democrats scored another major gubernatorial win in staunchly conservative Kansas, where the Democratic state senator Cindy Holscher narrowly defeated the Republican state senate president, Ty Masterson.
[ Democrats pledge to expose ‘absolute avalanche of corruption’ under Donald TrumpOpens in new window ]
Masterson, who received Trump’s endorsement, faced a campaign in which Holscher repeatedly highlighted his ties to the Republican president. At the same time, Holscher maintained that she would remain willing to co-operate with the Trump administration on issues where common ground could be found.
The back-to-back victories in Alaska and Kansas underscore the scale of Democratic gains in what has become a nationwide electoral shift.
The party’s long-anticipated “blue wave” has now materialised, with Democrats flipping eight seats in the US Senate, gaining more than two dozen seats in the House and significantly expanding their control of governors’ offices after the November 3rd midterms.
Such gains have handed Democrats a strong majority in Congress for the latter half of Trump’s second presidency, delivering a major shift in the balance of power in Washington and state governments across the US.
Meanwhile, with few ballots left to count for Alaska’s midterm US Senate election, Democrat Mary Peltola on Saturday was leading Republican incumbent Dan S Sullivan, Alaska Public Media reported. That had prompted MS Now to characterise that Senate race as “leans Democratic”.
Beside Alaska and Kansas, the Democratic Party won gubernatorial elections over Republicans in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas, putting them in control of a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010. Gina Hinojosa is the first Democrat to be elected governor of Texas in 35 years – and also the state’s first Hispanic governor.
A major factor in the GOP’s midterm defeat is the unpopularity of Trump, whom most Republican lawmakers clung to even as polls indicated voters did not support his immigration crackdown, tariffs, the war with Iran or his signature domestic policy bill. – The Guardian

Former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans, including one endorsed by President Donald Trump. His victory means Democrats will control the governor’s office in 30 states, including several they flipped after years of Republican control in places such as Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas.
Kreiss-Tomkins, often referred to as JKT, completed a political comeback three years after leaving the state House. He travelled throughout Alaska to build his coalition and focused on affordability, advocated for full funding of public schools and called for all oil and gas producers to pay corporate income tax. He also sought a moratorium on new data centres until state lawmakers pass regulations for their development.
He said Alaska had become “broken” under eight years of outgoing Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and needed a change. He cited, among other issues, a state ferry system that he said has been left in shambles, with routes to many communities cut drastically. The ferry is a key mode of transportation for southeast Alaska communities not connected by roads, some of which also have limited air service.
Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, emphasized a willingness to work across party lines and said he wanted a Cabinet with Republicans, Democrats and independents.
“If they’re competent, if they’re service-minded, if they’re entrepreneurial, if they’re problem solvers, you’re on the team. Game on,” he said during a candidate forum last month. “Let’s go, and let’s get Alaska back on track.”
Republican U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, who has at times been at odds with her party, including Trump, endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins a week before the election. She said Kreiss-Tomkins “understands that governing requires listening to people with different perspectives and finding common ground to solve the problems all of us face.”
Three former governors including Democrat Tony Knowles, independent Bill Walker and Republican Frank Murkowski, the senator’s father, also endorsed him.
In a statement declaring victory earlier Friday, Kreiss-Tomkins said voters wanted change and “a government that works across party lines to move Alaska forward. Our administration will not waste a single day getting to work to solve problems for Alaska.” He said his campaign had more than 10,000 donors.

His campaign did not immediately respond to requests for comment after The Associated Press called the race.
He defeated Republicans Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor. Trump had endorsed Wilson, a business owner, and criticized the other Republican candidates for staying in the race. Bronson is a former mayor of Anchorage, Alaska’s largest city, while Taylor was a state attorney-general under Dunleavy.
Bronson congratulated Kreiss-Tomkins on social media and wished him success. A message seeking comment from Wilson’s campaign was not immediately returned.
Many Republicans saw ranking as their party’s best shot of retaining the governor’s seat. It was a message that conflicted with that of Trump, who has consistently complained about Alaska’s unusual voting method, including during a rally in Alaska in October.
Kreiss-Tomkins finished first in August’s open primary, followed by a second Democrat, Tom Begich, who withdrew from the race. Begich’s campaign at the time said it had concluded that the “strongest path to victory is to bring Democratic voters, donors and resources together behind one candidate.” Wilson finished third in the primary.
Kreiss-Tomkins said compromise “is a virtue, not a dirty word,” and said he saw the mission of the new governor as working with lawmakers to resolve long-standing problems in the state.
The state’s last Democratic governor, Tony Knowles, left office in 2002 after serving back-to-back terms. Walker served from 2014 to 2018.
Kreiss-Tomkins will be sworn in Dec. 7. His lieutenant governor is Zac Johnson, an independent.

Republicans lost another big race, this one the governorship of Alaska, a state that also voted to keep the confusing ranked-choice voting system that is hated by pretty much everyone except Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and Democrats.
Former U.S. Representative Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins will win the northernmost state’s gubernatorial contest, beating out Republican candidate Bernadette Wilson and two others in the ranked-choice election, the first Democrat to hold the governor’s position in over 20 years and another flip for the left-wing party.

Also in the running were two other Republicans, Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson and the state’s former Attorney General Treg Taylor, a trio that some feared would split the GOP vote.
In his declaration of victory, Kreiss-Tomkins said that Alaskans had “voted for change” and pledged that “Our administration will not waste a single day getting to work to solve problems for Alaska.”
Kreiss-Tomkins had the endorsement of Murkowski, who crossed party lines to back the Democrat.
One of the issues he campaigned on was a moratorium on data centers, a winning issue for Democrats virtually everywhere that the GOP is on the wrong side of with voters.
“Across Alaska, Alaskans are concerned about data center development, while our state government has taken no steps to pass regulation or protect Alaskans,” he said in a statement. “We need a moratorium on all data centers until regulation can be passed.”
Kreiss-Tomkin is the first Democrat to be elected to lead the state since 1998, back when Bill Clinton was in the White House.

In Alaska, all candidates run on the same ballot for the primary regardless of their party; the top four candidates then move on to the general election where voters then rank them in order of preference. If no candidate goes over 50 percent on the first ballot, the decision then moves onto the ranked-choice system.
Ranked choice was narrowly approved by voters in 2020 and was implemented for the first time in 2022.
One prominent critic of ranked-choice voting in Alaska is President Donald J. Trump, who last month denounced it as a “TOTAL DEMOCRAT SCAM meant to confuse the Voter” in a post to Truth Social in which he also ripped Murkowski as “the Republicans’ Worst Senator, by far.”
Still uncertain is the other Alaska race that has drawn national attention, with Democrat Senate candidate Mary Peltola clinging to a lead over incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and two others, including the other Dan Sullivan, an independent former teacher who was allegedly recruited by Peltola staffers in a devious bit of political chicanery.
Trump has taken a very personal interest in the Alaska Senate contest, which, if the real Sullivan loses, will give the Democrats 56 seats in the upper chamber.

sources.news_title: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins Makes History With Alaska Victory
sources.text:
Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has defeated three Republican opponents to win Alaska’s gubernatorial election, making history in the traditionally red state and helping his party reach a milestone not seen in more than three decades.
His victory means Democrats will control 30 of America's 50 governorships for the first time since 1993, following a wave of gains in the November 3 midterm elections.
Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, will also become the first Alaska governor born after the state joined the Union in 1959, as well as its youngest-ever governor.
Read More on News
This year's midterms saw Democrats flip both the House and Senate, along with a slew of governors’ mansions, including victories in historic Republican strongholds as voters turned on President Donald Trump over issues such as the cost-of-living and war in Iran.
The Associated Press called the Alaska contest on Friday evening local time with Kreiss-Tomkins securing 50.8 percent of the vote, against 28.1 percent for Trump-endorsed opponent Bernadette Wilson.
Two other Republican candidates also ran; Dave Bronson who got 13.6 percent of the vote and Treg Taylor who secured 7.7 percent.
Why Alaska Didn't Need a Ranked-Choice Runoff
Unlike most other states, Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, allowing voters to rank candidates in order of preference and multiple candidates from the same party to compete. However, because Kreiss-Tomkins secured more than 50 percent of first-choice votes, he won outright without the need for additional rounds of vote counting.
Kreiss-Tomkins will replace the term-limited Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy who has served in the role since 2018.
Newsweek contacted the Kreiss-Tomkins, Wilson, Bronson and Taylor campaigns for comment by email on Saturday outside of regular office hours.
First Alaska Governor Born in State of Alaska
Kreiss-Tomkins’s victory will make him the first governor of Alaska to have been born in the state since it achieved statehood in 1959.
Previously there were two Alaska-born governors; Governor William Egan who served from 1959 to 1966 and Governor Bill Walker who held the office from 2014 to 2018. However both were born prior to Alaska getting statehood.
He will also be Alaska’s first Democratic governor since Tony Knowles, who was in office from 1994 to 2002.
At 37, he will become the youngest sitting governor in the United States when he takes office.
Democrats Reach 30 Governorships for First Time Since 1993
Kreiss-Tomkins' victory also marks a significant milestone for Democrats nationally, bringing their total number of governorships to 30 for the first time since 1993.
The party will control 60 percent of America's governorships next year, having flipped six Republican-held states in the midterm elections. Republicans had held a majority of governorships since 2010.
The Democratic gains in 2026 represent another setback for Republicans following their losses in Congress, giving the opposition party greater influence over state policymaking ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
Reactions To The Win
In a statement released on Friday after his victory was confirmed Kreiss-Tomkins said: “Alaskans voted for change and for a government that works across party lines to move Alaska forward.
“Thank you to every Alaskan who invited us into your home and to the 10,100 donors who gave to the campaign.”
Speaking to local media outlet Alaska Beacon on Friday second-placed Wilson said: “JKT was on top on election night, on top in the first round. He’s gonna be your governor.”
Referring to Kreiss-Tomkins she added: “I know that he genuinely cares about the state. We disagree very strongly on what looks like and how we get there, but I don’t look at him and think, ‘Oh my gosh, you’re some outsider guy who just moved here 10 years ago and now thinks you should be the governor.’”
Wilson argued having three rival Republican candidates vying for the governors office reduced the support they received from GOP donors.
She said: “The reality is, the Republican Party, the donors, you know, all of the conservative groups, they had the ability to suck the oxygen out of the room, even if other candidates do not want to withdraw.”
In a statement posted on social media Bronson congratulated Kreiss-Tomkins on his victory adding: “Alaskans have made their choice, and I respect their decision. It was a pleasure campaigning against him. I wish him all the success.”
Alaska's Other Major Election Remains Undecided
In the crunch Alaska Senate race incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan is behind Democrat Mary Peltola with 46.1 percent of the vote to her 49.8 percent with 96 percent reporting, though the race has yet to be called by the Associated Press.
Gerald L. Heikes, another Republican, is on 2.1 percent of the vote while independent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. has 1.6 percent of the vote. As neither candidate looks set to achieve 50 percent of the vote the contest is likely to be determined by ranked choice tabulation, with the worst performing candidates removed and their votes reallocated based on second preferences until there is a clear winner.
The presence of Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. in the race sparked intense controversy with Republicans arguing he only took part to take votes off Senator Sullivan due to confusion over their similar names.

Alaska elects Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins governor
sources.text:
Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state representative from the small island community of Sitka, won the race for Alaska governor, according to a race call by the Associated Press.
At 37, he’ll be the youngest governor in state history.
Kreiss-Tomkins will replace outgoing Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a term-limited Republican who has been governor since 2018. The state’s last Democratic governor was Tony Knowles, who left office in 2002.
Kreiss-Tomkins, known by his initials JKT, made his “high-energy, bipartisan, problem-solving approach” a centerpiece of his campaign.
He’s said he plans to build an administration of Democrats, Republicans and independents and described himself at a debate as a “man of the middle.” He was endorsed by three former governors — a Democrat, a Republican and an independent — along with Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski.
“Alaskans want change,” Kreiss-Tomkins said in an interview Friday. “They want (a) bipartisan problem-solving approach in their elected officials, and that's what they're going to get with me as governor.”
Kreiss-Tomkins is on track to win more than 50% of the first-choice vote, meaning the race would not be determined by ranked choice tabulation. The results remain unofficial until they’re certified; election officials plan to do so Nov. 25.
The AP race call came after 10 days of counting votes, including those coming in by mail and from remote parts of the state. In the ranked-choice system the state uses, he faced three Republican candidates, including one, business owner Bernadette Wilson, backed by President Trump.
Wilson acknowledged her loss in a phone interview with the Alaska Beacon Friday morning. She told the Beacon that despite deep disagreements on the best way forward for the state, she was glad someone born in the state had been elected to lead it. Neither Wilson nor her campaign has not responded to calls, texts or emails from Alaska Public Media since Election Day.
Another Republican in the race, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson, congratulated Kreiss-Tomkins on social media Friday.
“Alaskans have made their choice, and I respect their decision,” he said.
With Kreiss-Tomkins’ win and others in the midterms, Democrats will hold 30 governors’ offices across the country, up from 24 now.
Kreiss-Tomkins will take office in a state where voters have loudly complained that things aren’t working as they should.
Rising costs and relatively flat state funding have forced schools to close and class sizes to rise. Already-high costs for food, fuel and housing have risen sharply, and a looming shortage of easily accessible natural gas near the state’s population centers is threatening to push prices higher. And Alaskans have been migrating out of the state for more than a decade.
Plans to focus on ‘making government work’
Kreiss-Tomkins has offered glimpses of what his administration will bring in interviews and speeches since Election Day.
Speaking to the Resource Development Development Council in Anchorage on Wednesday, Kreiss-Tomkins listed his first priority as solving nuts-and-bolts problems — what he called “unsexy and non-glamorous” issues like wait times for state permits and government benefits like Medicaid. He said he hoped to “cultivate a culture of constant improvement in state government.”
“I really want to focus on making government work … making sure the basic processes and services that government is responsible for, that industry and others rely on, is working in the best possible way,” he said.
Kreiss-Tomkins has yet to announce any possible appointees to his administration, but hinted Wednesday that he might keep some Dunleavy administration commissioners. In an interview Friday, he declined to give specifics and said he expected to start naming appointees next week.
“It was probably pretty clear with our campaign what areas we felt Alaska needed to go in a different direction from the Dunleavy administration, and I think in those areas, correspondingly, you know, we will have new leadership,” he said.
The next governor is set to take office amid a war-driven boom in oil prices that could leave the state budget with a surplus in the hundreds of millions of dollars. An updated revenue forecast is due out next month.
Even so, Kreiss-Tomkins said he expects to propose a “moderate” Permanent Fund dividend and exercise what he described as “responsibility and restraint.”
Alaska’s dependence on oil revenue lends itself to a feast-or-famine dynamic, he said.
“I know what the famine cycle looks like because that basically described all 10 years I happened to be in the Legislature,” he said. “But I have seen the history of what the feast cycle looks like, and I really don't want the pendulum to swing too hard the other direction.”
In that vein, Kreiss-Tomkins said he’s planning to pursue an amendment to the state Constitution to place stricter limits on how much the state can withdraw from the Permanent Fund each year. And he said he wants to deposit some of the coming year’s possible surplus into the state’s rainy-day fund.
But as Kreiss-Tomkins said numerous times on the campaign trail, there’s one area where he says he would like to see more spending: education.

sources.news_title: JKT tops 50% of first-choice votes for Alaska governor, Republican opponents concede
sources.text:
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat, is declaring victory in Alaska’s gubernatorial election.
In results posted Thursday night by the Alaska Division of Elections, Kreiss-Tomkins had more than 50% of the first-choice votes for governor in this year’s election, putting him above the threshold for a ranked choice runoff.
CNN declared him the winner against three Republican challengers on Thursday night. The Associated Press has not yet called the race, and the Alaska Division of Elections is not scheduled to certify the result until Nov. 25. Preliminary final results are expected Nov. 18.
“It was a team effort every step of the way, and we always believed we could (win),” Kreiss-Tomkins said on Monday. “So it’s really really gratifying to have that official race call, or whatever CNN calls it, to kind of put some punctuation on the sentence.”
Kreiss-Tomkins was the lone Democrat in a field of four candidates seeking to replace Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who is term-limited and was unable to run for re-election this year. Dunleavy could run again in four years.
Even before Thursday, preliminary results indicated Kreiss-Tomkins would win the race even if it went to a ranked choice runoff.
Kreiss-Tomkins’ closest opponent in the election was Republican Bernadette Wilson, who had 28.7% of the 256,823 first-choice votes counted by the end of the day Thursday.
Republican candidate Dave Bronson was third, with 13.7% and Republican candidate Treg Taylor was fourth with 7.3%.
“Congratulations to Governor-elect Kreiss-Tomkins on winning the Alaska governor’s race with a majority of the vote,” Bronson said in a statement posted on his campaign Facebook page. “Alaskans have made their choice, and I respect their decision. It was a pleasure campaigning against him. I wish him all the success.”
By phone on Friday morning, Wilson said that while she was disappointed in the result and hoped for a different outcome as more ballots were counted, the trajectory since Election Day wasn’t a surprise.
“JKT was on top on election night, on top in the first round. He’s gonna be your governor,” she said.
Wilson and Kreiss-Tomkins were both born in Alaska, and Wilson said that while they disagree on policy, she is happy that someone from the state will be leading it.
“I know that he genuinely cares about the state. We disagree very strongly on what (caring for the state) looks like and how we get there, but I don’t look at him and think, ‘Oh my gosh, you’re some outsider guy who just moved here 10 years ago and now thinks you should be the governor.’ And so he’ll be just the third governor that was born here,” Wilson said.
Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, also will be the youngest governor in state history and the first Democrat since 2002, when Tony Knowles left office after an eight-year term.
No announcements on transition plan yet
Kreiss-Tomkins said he expects to announce the members of his transition team — the people who will help organize Alaska’s new government — early next week.
“Next week there will start to be a pretty steady cadence of updates and announcements from us,” he said.
Alaska’s constitution requires the new governor to be sworn into office at noon Dec. 7. Kreiss-Tomkins said he hasn’t yet decided a location for that event. He declined to say whether he’s thinking of Anchorage, Juneau, or Sitka, his hometown.
Dec. 15 is the statutory deadline for the new governor to present a draft budget. In 2018, when Dunleavy took over from former Gov. Bill Walker, he introduced a slightly modified version of a Walker proposal, then unveiled a major fiscal austerity plan in February, the deadline for the governor to submit amendments to the budget.
“There’s a lot to do, and we’re excited to get to work with an obsessive, problem-solving energy,” Kreiss-Tomkins said on Friday.
“We’re thinking about the budget next year, we’re thinking about building an administration and we’re thinking about a governing agenda, and each of those three things are big things, and taking them all apace now that there’s a little bit more clarity,” he said.
Kreiss-Tomkins will work with predominantly Democratic coalitions in the state House and Senate. The House coalition will have at least 24 members and could have as many as 27, depending on the result of close races where ballot counting is continuing.
The Senate coalition is expected to have a bare-minimum 11 members, including 8 Democrats, 2 Republicans and 1 independent.
Wilson explains her thoughts on why Republicans lost the election
Seventeen candidates registered for the primary election, including two Democrats, three independents and 12 Republicans.
In the primary, Kreiss-Tomkins finished with the most votes, followed by fellow Democrat Tom Begich, Wilson and Bronson.
Begich withdrew from the race in order to consolidate support behind Kreiss-Tomkins, which promoted fifth-place finisher Treg Taylor into the top four.
Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom disqualified Taylor, citing his failure to properly complete a financial disclosure form on time, but she reversed her decision days later.
The brief disqualification saw Taylor’s wife replace him on the ballot; she was removed once his candidacy was restored.
Wilson had the highest vote total among Republicans in the primary election. Before the primary, she had said that in order to consolidate support, she would quit the race if she wasn’t the top vote-getter.
Other Republicans made similar pledges, but Bronson and Taylor stayed in the race, pointing out that even if they withdrew, they would have simply been replaced by other Republicans who finished lower in the primary result.
With three Republicans on the ballot, the Alaska Republican Party and top Republican officials — including Dunleavy — generally declined to endorse one candidate or another and instead urged Republican candidates to “rank the red” by choosing Wilson, Taylor and Bronson in any order.
Wilson, by phone on Friday, said that wasn’t an effective strategy.
“The reality is, the Republican Party, the donors, you know, all of the conservative groups, they had the ability to suck the oxygen out of the room, even if other candidates do not want to withdraw,” Wilson said.
With three options to choose from, Republican donors stayed away or limited their financial help, Wilson said. Independent expenditure groups didn’t participate in the election to the degree that they did in 2022 or 2018, either.
While Kreiss-Tomkins is on track to win a majority of the first-choice votes for governor, Wilson believes that could have been different with more financial support and organization from Republicans.
“That’s why I say, even if JKT takes it on the first round, there’s no doubt in my mind that this is a very direct result of not being able to consolidate and collaborate, and that’s something that on the conservative side — we really got to look at ourselves in the mirror and figure out what we’re going to do here,” she said.
Wilson said she intends to stay active in Alaska politics — she has campaigned for conservative causes for almost two decades — but isn’t yet sure about her next steps.
At a statewide level, she urged Alaska conservatives to start immediately thinking about 2028, when incumbent Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, faces re-election.
According to historic primary election results, most registered Alaska Republicans oppose Murkowski and prefer a more conservative Republican, but Murkowski has been able to stay in office with the support of Democrats, moderate Republicans and independents.
Wilson, who opposes Murkowski, said that unless Republican organizations — including the state party — organize and back a single candidate in 2028, they risk a repeat of the vote dilution that happened this year.

Kreiss-Tomkins led the field in August’s open primary, with fellow Democrat Tom Begich finishing second. Begich later withdrew, saying his campaign had determined that the “strongest path to victory is to bring Democratic voters, donors and resources together behind one candidate.” Wilson placed third in the primary.
Kreiss-Tomkins has described compromise as “a virtue, not a dirty word” and said the next governor must work with lawmakers to address Alaska’s longstanding challenges.
Alaska’s last Democratic governor, Tony Knowles, left office in 2002 after serving two consecutive terms. Walker was governor from 2014 to 2018.
Kreiss-Tomkins will take office on Dec. 7. His lieutenant governor will be Zac Johnson, an independent.
